Balance is defined by the usefulness of individual cards. Can I use a Torn
Signpost or a Govern the Unaligned or whatever at all - or is it too useful and
easy to win with on the other hand? Just because you can envision a particular
type of deck, for instance a "rush combat" deck or an "intercept combat" deck or
something, doesn't mean game balance demands that that type of deck be viable to
play. Otherwise, people will come up with all sorts of decks they would like to
see become being playable: Corruption decks, deck destruction (i.e. The
Slaughterhouse) decks, decks based on allies, decks based entirely on master
cards, etc. The question is more about whether various types of offensive
combat cards can be considered useful in the game in some type of functional
deck or not.

Fred

Messages.Author: Nystulc

Awazzzz wrote, in response to LSJ:

>Balance? I thought the general feeling was that bleed/vote decks did better
>than combat decks - and the rule gives more cost to cards like Daring the
>Dawn.

I think the strategy you have in mind for promoting "balance" is flawed. Your
idea is that the deficiencies of combat decks is to permit the existence of a
handful of overpowered cards.

This might "balance" combat compared to S&B, but it would not balance the card
set. Rather, it would create a situation where ONLY a certain narrow type of
combat deck is viable for play, and most combat cards become wallpaper. It
also creates a situation where, in a competitive environment, all combat
defence will be directed against aggravated damage combat decks, resulting in a
distressing sameness even in non-combat decks..

If you want to improve "balance", it is better to do so in ways that keep all
combat cards playable. If you want to help combat decks become more viable,
then it is best to make a change that will work well with a larger variety of
old combat cards and decks.

I like the approach of the design team better than yours. One of the things
they are rumoured have done is weaken Majesty. This increases the odds for all
combat decks, and makes a large variety of combat cards more likely to see
play, whereas your approach enables only a small variety of combat decks, and
pushes the remainder deeper into the margins.

Another thing they have done (not a rumor) is to further enable weapon decks by
making Concealed Weapon disciplineless. By creating one balanced, playable
card, they make a whole host of combat cards (particularly weapons and allies)
somewhat more balanced and playable than they once were.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <20020720040412...@mb-mf.aol.com>, Awazzzz

<awa...@aol.com> writes:
>Yeah, I really do think that it would make the game more balanced. I played
>with this rule back when V:TES came out and liked it alot. Back then, yes
>vampires actually got burned.

I think what you meant to write in your first sentence wasn't
"balanced", rather more "brutal" or similar.

In Jyhad it was *impossible*, that is *absolutely impossible*, for a
Gangrel to burn a vampire with a single poke - even with any other
damage sources - or for an Ivory Bow to do the same.

It was *just* possible for a Flamethrower to do it. And the cards were
balanced by having the Flamethrower cost a *LOT* more pool. Thus the
cards were balanced relative to one another.

(Another example of the wrong changes made in V:TES was that, under NO
circumstances was it possible for Pulled Fangs to *EVER* burn someone
under Jyhad. That is how the card was designed and costed. It was
probably still too powerful, even with a torporise effect. (It was
damage, and so could be prevented, unlike Paralyse.))

Burning vampires != measure of balance.

Combat decks already command a great deal of power by targeting
secondary resources - specifically, vampires, sometimes allies. They
form the basis of the original lock down decks. If you run in, knock a
vampire into torpor and repeat - which is easily possible - the deck
gets shut down. It can rebuild itself, if it can rescue its vampires,
but such isn't easy anyway. (2 blood and another vampire is a
significant cost.)

Also, the Bloodhunt is a huge balancing factor in terms of combat.
(Well, mostly combat. It is possible to torporise vampires outside of
combat, and diablerie doesn't occur in combat always - Amaranth being
the main way to do it in combat - but it's a large factor towards
balancing combative arrangements.) A combative deck will suffer - and
was intended to suffer - by having less access to votes. Having to
conspire with a voting deck to back it up in the Bloodhunt, or to
convince the voting deck to do the diablerie itself, provides a measure
of balance. Burning is harder, but evades the Bloodhunt. Being able to
evade it with a single point of aggravated damage is not significantly
harder.

The Brujah could pound you for *lots* of damage, and you'd go to torpor.
The Gangrel could do it with just one card - a claw - but that makes it
much easier for you to prevent. Neither clan had easy access to
burning, nor was it meant to. (Bear in mind how expensive Burning Wrath
is, for example.)

Combat is, effectively, the original "lock down" deck. Forget
Reality/Sensory Deprivation, or whatever. You torporise vampires, they
can't do anything. That's it. They bring out another, you torporise
it. Again. Again. And again.

>There's no inherent risk of being
>at 0 blood, most of the agg cards cannot burn a vamp!

Correct, for the most part. That's how the game was designed, balanced
and costed, way back in the beginning.

A desire to make combat more powerful is *not* the same as making
vampires easier to burn being balanced.

First of all, you need to demonstrate that combat needs empowering,
because it is significantly unbalanced. Certain facets of combat do
very well, thank you. A broad increase in power levels is not a very
useful way to target such changes. Gangrel Royalty decks can do
extremely well. Brujah pot/cel decks can do very well similarly. (It's
notable in the latter case that changes to Majesty won't affect it
heavily, because it *already* combats Majesty itself. This is how
targeted changes can be useful employed.)

Then you need to demonstrate that making vampires easier to burn is the
way to establish that balance. It's worth bearing in mind the assorted
effects that also deal aggravated damage which would also be affected by
such a change.

I'd suggest using Google to dig up many of the previous arguments. I'd
also suggest examining the ways in which targeted action can be
significantly more subtle. (For instance, a rewrite of Majesty does not
affect Daring the Dawn.) Then I'd suggest working out the difference
between "simple" and "balanced" - if you can rewrite a sentence, without
effort, from "This is more simple, do this" to "This is more balanced,
do this", regarding a delicate, complex issue, then you have probably
made some significant errors of logic.



easy anyway. (2 blood and another vampire is a significant cost.)

Then why wallpaper S:CE?

>>Also, the Bloodhunt is a huge balancing factor in terms of combat. (Well,
mostly combat. It is possible to torporise vampires outside of combat, and
diablerie doesn't occur in combat always - Amaranth being
the main way to do it in combat - but it's a large factor towards balancing
combative arrangements.) A combative deck will suffer - and was intended to
suffer - by having less access to votes. Having to
conspire with a voting deck to back it up in the Bloodhunt, or to convince the
voting deck to do the diablerie itself, provides a measure of balance. Burning
is harder, but evades the Bloodhunt. Being able to
evade it with a single point of aggravated damage is not significantly harder.

The bloodhunt helps those with votes. - not combatants.

>>The Brujah could pound you for *lots* of damage, and you'd go to torpor. The
Gangrel could do it with just one card - a claw - but that makes it much easier
for you to prevent. Neither clan had easy access to burning, nor was it meant
to. (Bear in mind how expensive Burning Wrath is, for example.)

There are Gangrels with potence and Brujas with Protean, so I really don't see
your point. There is also Gangrel Revel. LSJ would like you to believe that
this rule is in place because of balance, but really the only reason he made it
was to return to the original rules structure.

>>Combat is, effectively, the original "lock down" deck. Forget
Reality/Sensory Deprivation, or whatever. You torporise vampires, they can't
do anything. That's it. They bring out another, you torporise it. Again.
Again. And again.

If I have just brought a vamp out, it has plenty of blood, so this rule does
not directly effect the lockdown deck. A vampire in torpor with no blood is
just as locked as a burned vamp. Should we errata Sense Dep to only tap
vampires for a turn? No!!

>>Correct, for the most part. That's how the game was designed, balanced and
costed, way back in the beginning.

Then why did they change it for V:TES?

>>A desire to make combat more powerful is *not* the same as making vampires
easier to burn being balanced.

No, But making vampires easier to burn would make combat more balanced. Again,
this is a better way than wallpapering cards.

>>First of all, you need to demonstrate that combat needs empowering, because
it is significantly unbalanced. Certain facets of combat do very well, thank
you. A broad increase in power levels is not a very useful way to target such
changes. Gangrel Royalty decks can do extremely well. Brujah pot/cel decks
can do very well similarly. (It's notable in the latter case that changes to
Majesty won't affect it
heavily, because it *already* combats Majesty itself. This is how targeted
changes can be useful employed.)

I personally do not think combat decks are underpowered. I just think that
most people think so. I think that WW is trying to empower combat decks for
this reason. Balance has to do with cards in a game, not the rules of it. The
rules effect the balance of the cards. Changing a card's text effects its
balance. Since when has Majesty been a broken card? I have been playing this
game for years and you mean to tell me the whole time I am getting gyped by
people that play majesty? -that majesty has somehow been ruining the game?
Personally, I have been having fun for the last number of years with the game,
I'm sorry that it was ruined for you.

>>Then you need to demonstrate that making vampires easier to burn is the way
to establish that balance. It's worth bearing in mind the assorted effects
that also deal aggravated damage which would also be affected by such a change.

AGAIN, there are two ways this rule would effect the game. First, it would
increase the cost of cards that use agg damage as a cost, second it would
increase the effect of cards that used agg damage as an effect. Cards that use
agg as a cost are generaly (but not limited to) actions/action modifiers.

>>I'd suggest using Google to dig up many of the previous arguments. I'd also
suggest examining the ways in which targeted action can be significantly more
subtle. (For instance, a rewrite of Majesty does not
affect Daring the Dawn.) Then I'd suggest working out the difference between
"simple" and "balanced" - if you can rewrite a sentence, without effort, from
"This is more simple, do this" to "This is more balanced,
do this", regarding a delicate, complex issue, then you have probably made some

significant errors of logic. I think what you meant to write in your first

sentence wasn't "balanced", rather more "brutal" or similar.

James, please do not assume that I do not know what I am talking about. I have
participated in many threads on discussion, particularly during 7/7 when this
rule was made. Making things less brutal - or wimpy - effects balance just as
making things brutal does. Personally, I prefer brutal games to wimpy ones.

Nystylc:

>>I think the strategy you have in mind for promoting "balance" is flawed.
Your idea is that the deficiencies of combat decks is to permit the existence
of a handful of overpowered cards.

Which cards?

>>This might "balance" combat compared to S&B, but it would not balance the
card set. Rather, it would create a situation where ONLY a certain narrow type
of combat deck is viable for play, and most combat cards become wallpaper. It
also creates a situation where, in a competitive environment, all combat
defence will be directed against aggravated damage combat decks, resulting in a
distressing sameness even in non-combat decks..

Non agg damage is not effected by the rule. Hitting someone for 9 points of
non-agg damage is still a powerful thing

>>If you want to improve "balance", it is better to do so in ways that keep all
combat cards playable. If you want to help combat decks become more viable,
then it is best to make a change that will work well with a larger variety of
old combat cards and decks.

This change does improve a number of combat cards - the agg-damage ones. Let
me get my point straight: Combat decks ARE effective, and this rule would help
them, but not make them OVERpowered.

>>I like the approach of the design team better than yours. One of the things

Majesty is not a broken card. I have been playing with and against Majesty for

>>Another thing they have done (not a rumor) is to further enable weapon decks
by making Concealed Weapon disciplineless. By creating one balanced, playable
card, they make a whole host of combat cards (particularly weapons and allies)

somewhat more balanced and playable than they once were. I think the strategy

you have in mind for promoting "balance" is flawed. Your idea is that the
deficiencies of combat decks is to permit the existence of a handful of
overpowered cards.

Instead of changing Concealed weapon, they could have made a new card. This
way, my old CW would still be playable as written, and I would not have to try

In message <20020720145809...@mb-fa.aol.com>, Awazzzz

<awa...@aol.com> writes:
>James Coupe:
>
>>>I think what you meant to write in your first sentence wasn't "balanced",
>rather more "brutal" or similar.
>
>I think that a game about vampires should be somewhat "brutal" Vampires are
>not nice people.

Some vampires are not nice people, in the V:tM world. Perhaps the
majority.

It is also notable, however, the vampires are super human in their
*defensive* capabilities. Just as they can dish out damage, they can
also take a lot - bashing damage is halved, lethal damage is soakable
under the right conditions. (V:TES simplifies this, of course.)

>Just because something is brutal, does not mean it is not
>balanced. People on this newsgroup cry when they get their asses kicked and so
>they tone the game down to appease them.

This is based on faulty premises, and is fundamentally flawed.

So far as I can see, rules are not changed to "appease" people.
Whenever I have corresponded with LSJ regarding rulings or rules changes
where I have had a problem with a specific section of the set-up, very
little has been weighed in the balance of "appeasing" people.

If a situation is unbalanced, inconsistent or unclear, action is taken.
(Obviously, this is all in the view of LSJ and, presumably, the Rules
Team.)

People "crying" has never resulted in action being taken that I have
ever seen. People presenting logical, thoughtful, well-planned, well-
argued points of view, backed up with theory and practise in multiple
situations, has resulted in action being taken - not all of which I
necessarily agree with entirely, but corrective action nonetheless.

>Bleed has been toned down by rules,

Actually, bleed has been touched very little by the rules. Only No
Repeat Actions significantly touches it, and that is a specific subset
of bleed - bleed *and* untap. Many bleed decks don't untap (though,
equally, some do or would do if NRA didn't exist in some form or other)
and so are relatively untouched by this.

The rulings (in the general sense of all E/R/C together) on Deflection's
wording, later incorporated into recent printings, also made bleed more
powerful, relatively, since bleed bounce became harder to cycle. (Prior
to the changes, you could "cycle" a bleed bounce card by playing it,
selecting yourself as the target when you already were.) This makes
bleed bounce quite a lot weaker in the end game (though closer to
designer intent, almost certainly so), clogging the hand. Cycling
becomes a necessity.

Attempts to argue that Return to Innocence was balanced, however, are
likely to meet with failure and repeated rebuttals.

>vote has been toned down by rules,

Votes have been toned down in some respects - mostly that of vote
pushing. This tones down some specific vote decks, which were able to
exploit a facet that no other deck could - using one card type to do all
their things. Combat required rush and damage (or equipment or
whatever). Bleed required bleed actions and modifiers and stealth.
Votes could just call themselves, and pass themselves with the same
resource, as well as cycling hugely to no effect.

In part, this depowered some specific vote types - a lot of non-Presence
decks find life harder, though there are certain obvious exceptions (the
Lasombra, for instance).

Also, Presence oriented vote decks are very powerful. The Setites can
do some wholly evil things with votes.

Legacy of Pander - which may be one other sticking point - was returned
to its originally intended, designed, balanced and costed format. (The
text issued in The Sabbat was erroneous.)

>and combat has been toned down.

Combat has been refocused in some ways.

Some specific parts of combat have been made harder. Specifically,
aggravate damage is *closer* to the Jyhad rules. (The Jyhad rules are
quite complex, however.) However, in other matters, combat was never
touched by NRA if multiple ways of entering combat were available.
Strike: Combat Ends has been provided with multiple counters or
alternatives. Pulled Fangs was downgraded, but Concealed Weapon is to
be reprinted, making weapon decks more viable.

Swings and roundabouts. Combat has certainly gained in many ways -
Fame, for instance.

>Toning down
>a game does little for balancing and detracts from the excitement of the game.

Detracting from the "excitement" is a personal issue - this is not one
that can be argued.

Toning down doing little for balancing is a different issue, however.
First of all, it is necessary to demonstrate that different elements are
"toned down", and that they haven't advanced since through new cards.
Second of all, it is necessary to demonstrate that toning down doesn't
balance the game.

>This game will never have perfect balance.

This does not mean that balance is not a useful goal.

>However, I think that toning
>everything's power down to the level of wall paper cards is unacceptable.

That's fine, then.

Not everything is wallpaper, and substantial portions of the card set
see regular play, so that's fine.

>Also, we used to play with this rule, and I never found it particularly brutal.

You are one group. One group is welcome, on its own, to do whatever it
wants.

Specific gaming groups will almost always represent atypical sections of
the game. Do you play more vote? Do you play more combat? Do you play
more bleed? Do the Setites Corrupt a lot more often? Whatever.

For instance, if you regularly play combat decks in your gaming group,
it is possible that a lot of damage prevention creeps in. (This is only
one of many potential situations.) As such, the relative power of
certain cards will be skewed relative to a cross-play-group norm. Cards
that can be readily (in a specific play-group) defended against will not
necessarily be defensible in a non-skewed play-group. Drifts towards
strategy and counter-strategy being the only viable types have
threatened to kill the game before.

>>>In Jyhad it was *impossible*, that is *absolutely impossible*, for a Gangrel
>to burn a vampire with a single poke - even with any other damage sources - or
>for an Ivory Bow to do the same. It was *just* possible for a Flamethrower to
>do it. And the cards were balanced by having the Flamethrower cost a *LOT*
>more pool. Thus the cards were balanced relative to one another.
>
>Yes, and so the rules team changed the rule for V:TES - it was changed back
>when LSJ became the 1 man rules team in 7/7.

No, this fundamentally misunderstands the situation.

1) Regarding the 7/7 as a change back to the Jyhad rules is
fundamentally mistaken. Learning the rules changes may help.

2) LSJ is not and was not a one man rules team.

>Right now I cannot burn a vampire
>with a starshell grenade launcher - a grenade launcher cannot burn the vamp no
>matter how many times you hit it. This is silly.

Vampires are inherently tough creatures. They can resist huge amounts
of damage, and heal huge amounts of damage too. Only the Changing
Breeds can really outpace them with regards such.

>>>(Another example of the wrong changes made in V:TES was that, under NO
>circumstances was it possible for Pulled Fangs to *EVER* burn someone under
>Jyhad. That is how the card was designed and costed. It was probably still
>too powerful, even with a torporise effect. (It was damage, and so could be
>prevented, unlike Paralyse.))
>
>Sorry, James but one could do as much damage as one wanted with PF because it
>was not limited to one per combat

So?

Do you understand the Jyhad rules? It seems not. It would *probably*
aid you to research the Jyhad rules, as it would avoid such obvious
mistakes regarding the design and balance of those rules.

Under the Jyhad rules, it was impossible to *EVER* burn a vampire with
Pulled Fangs. This is because of the packeting system that existed for
damage. Of every packet of damage, the first point of aggravated damage
sent the vampire to torpor, irrespective of whether they were there
already or currently on their way to torpor. Thus, playing 20 Pulled
Fangs sent the vampire to torpor twenty times. The amount of damage
done was irrelevant. (With the exception of Franciscus' special
"ability".)

It was *impossible* to burn a vampire with Pulled Fangs, unless you
added another effect - such as a diablerie action or a copy of Amaranth.

>>>Burning vampires != measure of balance.
>
>It effects the balance of cards, yes

You misread the statement.

Burning vampires is not the same as a measure of balance. Just because
it would be easier to burn vampires under your proposed change, this
does not make it a useful measure of balance.

You have not demonstrated that burning vampires is necessary. You have
not demonstrated that combat is underpowered. You have not demonstrated
that combat will benefit from being upgraded in such a fashion, without
detriment. (For instance, whilst one type of aggravated damage deck
might remain balanced under your proposed change, there may be others
which do not.)

>>>Combat decks already command a great deal of power by targeting secondary
>resources - specifically, vampires, sometimes allies. They form the basis of
>the original lock down decks. If you run in, knock a
>vampire into torpor and repeat - which is easily possible - the deck gets shut
>down. It can rebuild itself, if it can rescue its vampires, but such isn't
>easy anyway. (2 blood and another vampire is a significant cost.)
>
>Then why wallpaper S:CE?

This is based on the premise that S:CE has been wallpapered.

There is no evidence to suggest from where I stand that S:CE has been
wallpapered.

"Then why wallpaper S:CE" is an excellent sound-bite. But you need to
put in a lot of work to show that it's been wallpapered. There are
certain specific sources of Strike: Combat Ends which may have been
addressed, or may be addressed in the Camarilla Edition (about which I
have no knowledge other than the vague rumours circulating), but other
sources of S:CE have been introduced at the same time.

Taking TheLasombra's Tournament Winning Deck Archive, the winner of
Thadius Zho: Boston includes 9 copies of Majesty. "Can I wear this
jacket too?" includes 6 Form of Mist, which depend on Strike: Combat
Ends being viable. Jay's deck from Origins 2002 includes 22 copies of
Earth Meld. That's looking at the first few decks.

You have not demonstrated that S:CE has been wallpapered. It would aid
you greatly if you would do so.

>>>Also, the Bloodhunt is a huge balancing factor in terms of combat. (Well,
>mostly combat. It is possible to torporise vampires outside of combat, and
>diablerie doesn't occur in combat always - Amaranth being
>the main way to do it in combat - but it's a large factor towards balancing
>combative arrangements.) A combative deck will suffer - and was intended to
>suffer - by having less access to votes. Having to
>conspire with a voting deck to back it up in the Bloodhunt, or to convince the
>voting deck to do the diablerie itself, provides a measure of balance. Burning
>is harder, but evades the Bloodhunt. Being able to
>evade it with a single point of aggravated damage is not significantly harder.
>
>The bloodhunt helps those with votes. - not combatants.

Erm, yes. That's the point.

Combatants are ****supposed**** to be hindered by the bloodhunt.

Being able to torporise vampires is supposed to be significantly easier
than burning a vampire outright. Thus burning a vampire via a diablerie
action (or Amaranth) includes difficulties of surviving a bloodhunt.

The game was *designed* to benefit from a mixture of strategies.
Richard Garfield says so. (Arguing about the design of Jyhad, specific
to the Jyhad incarnation, is much simplified if you read Richard
Garfield's own words on the situation.)

Providing a significant difficulty for combat decks allows a vote deck
to interact at this point. Thus diplomacy and inter-player balance are
established (or are sought to be established). The game then isn't a
situation of 5 different players trying to pull off five different
strategies with minimal interaction - it isn't supposed to be. Intra-
table diplomacy and balance is supposed to be achievable, though limited
in certain fashions - the predator-prey mechanism driving a lot of
motivation in diplomacy, such that few are the situations where two
players can both equally benefit from the same situation to the fullest
extent.

You still need to demonstrate that combatants need help. Aggravated
damage is not the only combat, and you have yet to even demonstrate that
aggravated damage based combat needs help.

You *have* provided your view that vampires should explode more often.
You are entitled to that view, and can play however you want in your
group. However, changes are made regarding pan-game balance, not just
individual groups. Some groups can, do and will exploit sources of
imbalance where they exist. Not all groups see all problems.

>>>The Brujah could pound you for *lots* of damage, and you'd go to torpor. The
>Gangrel could do it with just one card - a claw - but that makes it much easier
>for you to prevent. Neither clan had easy access to burning, nor was it meant
>to. (Bear in mind how expensive Burning Wrath is, for example.)
>
>There are Gangrels with potence and Brujas with Protean, so I really don't see
>your point.

This is unfortunate. :( Understanding costing, opportunity costs and
the balance they can provide is pretty fundamental to arguments of
cross-game balance. (Simplicity, designer intent, theme, limited
resources (both pool and library wise), uniqueness and so on are other
useful themes to explore.)

Yes, there are Gangrels with Potence - but these are not readily
available, such as Protean is.

The cheapest vampire with Potence available is a 6 capacity. (Indeed,
there are two vampires - Zack and Badger.) There are no Gangrel with
superior Potence, which doubles the effectiveness of many such cards.
(Resetting damage with Torn Signpost provides an additional 1 damage in
most situations at pot, but an additional 2 damage at POT. Undead
Strength provides +1 damage at pot, but +2 damage.)

For the Brujah, there is one Brujah with Protean - Don Cruez, a 10
capacity vampire.

What does this mean? It means that accessing these disciplines becomes
difficult, relative to accessing Protean. Pot/Pro is a *wonderful*
discipline combination. Quick Meld (excellent maneuvers), Flesh of
Marble (useful damage prevention, with an unfortunate Achilles Heel),
Immortal Grapple (preventing S:CE and equipment), Torn Signpost/Undead
Strength (providing significant amounts of damage) and a Claw (Claws of
the Dead, Bone Spur etc.) provide a formidable arsenal.

However, generating the vampires to unleash this arsenal is tricky.
It's expensive - large vampires, relative to a pot/cel type deck of 3
caps and similar. It's slow - if you go first, Zack North will take 3
turns to get out, assuming you don't have/draw Information Highway or
similar.

>There is also Gangrel Revel. LSJ would like you to believe that
>this rule is in place because of balance, but really the only reason he made it
>was to return to the original rules structure.

Gangrel Revel is fragile and expensive. 3 pool for +1 strength is a lot
of pool. It can also be immediately burned, assuming you aren't playing
against a Ravnos deck (who have good defences anyway). It is a master
card, and so competes for generally scarce Master Phase Actions.
(Certainly, the end game may become drawn out in terms of turns, but
many games are won or lost during the frenzy of earlier turns.)

>>>Combat is, effectively, the original "lock down" deck. Forget
>Reality/Sensory Deprivation, or whatever. You torporise vampires, they can't
>do anything. That's it. They bring out another, you torporise it. Again.
>Again. And again.
>
>If I have just brought a vamp out, it has plenty of blood, so this rule does
>not directly effect the lockdown deck.

This is a statement based mostly on inexperience of effective combat
decks.

In essence, a blood buffer should not prevent a combat deck from sending
you to torpor, if they're playing well. A potence deck will throw down
Disarm. A Gangrel deck will torporise you with a single claw. Breath
of the Dragon or Chiropteran Marauder (or whatever) from the Tzimisce.

*Of course*, you can defend. You can Dodge. You can prevent. You can
fight back, whatever. However, if a combat deck is in combat with you
and is having problems working out "Assuming my opponent doesn't play
any cards, how do I torporise them this combat?", something is probably
going significantly wrong - this may be down to luck of the draw, of
course.

Getting through blood on a vampire should be the least of a combat
deck's worries - cards for it should either be available in abundance,
or irrelevant. Targeting the right vampire (Are you rushing? How do
you stop blocks? How do you stop Obedience? Are you blocking? How do
you beat Change of Target?) and beating defence (what do I do if you
Skin of Steel? what do I do if you hit me with Lucky Blow? what do I
do if you have an Elysium: the Arboretum available) are significant
worries.

>A vampire in torpor with no blood is
>just as locked as a burned vamp. Should we errata Sense Dep to only tap
>vampires for a turn? No!!

Again, a bizarre extension of a line of reasoning.

Sensory Deprivation is very different to torporisation. And an
efficient combat deck both can and will torporise you with ease. If it
does it efficiently enough, you won't stay there for one turn - because
there won't be anyone to get you out.

>>>Correct, for the most part. That's how the game was designed, balanced and
>costed, way back in the beginning.
>
>Then why did they change it for V:TES?

A number of things changed for V:TES.

Partly, it is obvious that the changes for V:TES were designed to
streamline some elements of the game - wrongly assuming that such
streamlining wouldn't affect the balance of such cards. Jyhad was,
rightly, perceived as being extremely subtle and complex - attempts to
put it forward as a card game that anyone could be taught in ten minutes
were being made. The "Basic Game" is evidence of such.

One might also point to some of the textual changes that were made that
similarly shifted cards in ways they didn't expect.

It is also notable that your question elides certain facts:

"Then why did they change it for V:TES?" Who is they? The they for
Jyhad is not the same as the they for V:TES.

It is certainly obvious that the "they" who designed and "balanced"
Return to Innocence prior to its printing, and similarly Thoughts
Betrayed and Tomb of Rameses, were not terribly familiar with the game
as she was played properly. The "they" responsible for V:TES was
similarly removed from the "they" for Jyhad, in terms of understanding
the subtle balances that Jyhad had developed.

>>>A desire to make combat more powerful is *not* the same as making vampires
>easier to burn being balanced.
>
>No, But making vampires easier to burn would make combat more balanced. Again,
>this is a better way than wallpapering cards.

You have not shown that combat is unbalanced.

You have not shown that making vampires easier to burn would make combat
more balanced.

You have not shown that cards are being wallpapered.

Please provide proof, not soundbites. Simply *saying* that combat is
unbalanced does not make it so. Combat decks are doing well when played
well.

>>>First of all, you need to demonstrate that combat needs empowering, because
>it is significantly unbalanced. Certain facets of combat do very well, thank
>you. A broad increase in power levels is not a very useful way to target such
>changes. Gangrel Royalty decks can do extremely well. Brujah pot/cel decks
>can do very well similarly. (It's notable in the latter case that changes to
>Majesty won't affect it
>heavily, because it *already* combats Majesty itself. This is how targeted
>changes can be useful employed.)
>
>I personally do not think combat decks are underpowered.

Then they do not need to be upgraded.

If you do not think them underpowered, please do not argue for them to
be upgraded. You would then be arguing for them to be overpowered.

>I just think that
>most people think so.

Please point to these "most people". A statistically valid survey will
do.

>I think that WW is trying to empower combat decks for
>this reason. Balance has to do with cards in a game, not the rules of it.

Balance can derive from both cards and rules, as they interact with one
another.

For instance, the rules on discarding balance certain facets of the
game. You cannot just cycle through your deck endlessly, deck
composition becomes a huge facet of the game rather than something to be
worked at but then ignored in game if you messed up.

>The
>rules effect the balance of the cards. Changing a card's text effects its
>balance. Since when has Majesty been a broken card?

You may do well to read the archives on Google to see different views,
some of which I agree with, some of which I don't, but all of which have
some basis in different opinions and playgroups.

You may also do well to note that not all card text changes occur due to
brokenness. If Majesty was broken, errata would have been issued to it,
similar to that issued to Return to Innocence (which was later banned).

>I have been playing this
>game for years and you mean to tell me the whole time I am getting gyped by
>people that play majesty? -that majesty has somehow been ruining the game?

Many people play V:TES for years without seeing certain facets, certain
combinations.

The base set is intended to be balanced. Majesty has certainly been at
the very top end of the power curve for some time. A base set provides
a useful opportunity for rebalancing it.

If Majesty is the card you believe has been "wallpapered", you would do
well to examine the rumours more carefully. A simple cost of 1 blood
does little to wallpaper Majesty. It is certainly playable with such a
cost.

>Personally, I have been having fun for the last number of years with the game,
>I'm sorry that it was ruined for you.

Who said anything about ruined?

If I didn't enjoy V:TES, I wouldn't put so much time into it.

>>>Then you need to demonstrate that making vampires easier to burn is the way
>to establish that balance. It's worth bearing in mind the assorted effects
>that also deal aggravated damage which would also be affected by such a change.
>
>AGAIN, there are two ways this rule would effect the game.

You may want to learn the difference between "effect" and "affect",
since the two have distinct meanings, both of which can be applied in
such discussions, which may cause confusion. You appear, here, to mean
"affect".

>First, it would
>increase the cost of cards that use agg damage as a cost, second it would
>increase the effect of cards that used agg damage as an effect. Cards that use
>agg as a cost are generaly (but not limited to) actions/action modifiers.

Would you please provide a detailed analysis of these changes, in order
to support a case for them being both necessary *and* balanced?

>James, please do not assume that I do not know what I am talking about.

Thus far you have:

- shown ignorance of costing issues, regarding vampire creation and
discipline availability (Gangrel having Potence doesn't suddenly
make things magically happen, when it's only available on
specific large vampires, at inferior)

- confused soundbites of opinion with facts

- fundamentally misrepresented the Jyhad aggravated damage rules, whilst
also arguing for a separate set

- misrepresented the Rules Team as being one person

- claimed that combat decks aren't underpowered, but then argued for
them to be upgraded

- claimed that blood on a vampire alone will protect them from a combat
deck, which is not supported by real life facts

- claimed that Strike: Combat Ends has been wallpapered, without
providing evidence

- misunderstood the balance of cards like Gangrel Revel, which include
expense, opportunity cost and fragility in their balance

- confused your personal preferences with a need for rewrites

- argued that balance is only governed by cards, not the rules, when
both may have subtle roles to play

I can list more, if you want.

>I have
>participated in many threads on discussion, particularly during 7/7 when this
>rule was made. Making things less brutal - or wimpy - effects balance just as
>making things brutal does. Personally, I prefer brutal games to wimpy ones.

Your personal preferences are your own.

However, the game is not designed to be a combat game. It is a mix of
combat, bleed, politics, random actions, blocks, diplomacy, luck, skill
and cunning.

Combat is but one facet amongst many.

Rebalancing the game towards combat then balances it away from all the
other facets that exist.

>Nystylc:

Please note, it is generally considered to be good Usenet etiquette to
respond to posts individually.

This is why the References: header exists, so that a thread of replies
can be established.

If you would care to re-write this facet of Usenet, you can contribute
to USEFOR. However, whilst Usenet exists how it is - which is
emphatically not a random web-based discussion board, with random lists
of posts - respecting its mechanisms may aid you.

Messages.Author: Awazzzz
Messages.Body:
>>I consider vampires being easily burned a bad thing. It would be different
if you could correlate the likelihood to the size of the vampire. As it is,
losing a weenie may be insignificant but losing one of three (for instance)

minions you bring out is crippling. I consider vampires being easily burned a

bad thing. It would be different if you could correlate the likelihood to the
size of the vampire. As it is, losing a weenie may be insignificant but losing
one of three (for instance) minions you bring out is crippling.

Larger vampires would still be less likely to burn than small ones because they
have more blood.

>>Then why don't you play with your own little house rule and leave the rest of
us alone?

I am not going to play with CE, but there still needs to be rules that the game
is played by. I would rather make one rule change than so many card errata or
rewords.

>>I actually really like the idea of making Majesty cost a blood. I've pushed
for more ways for combat to counter S:CE but making the cost of playing S:CE
more prohibitive seems reasonable to me. How many PRE decks will be able to
afford the cost of Majesty-ing out of every combat now? They'll have to be more
selective in how they avoid combat when constructing a deck. (I'm thinking that
maneuvers will start to become more popular actually... I've already started
using them quite a bit)

Personally, I already use maneuvers in my combat decks. Now let's look at S:CE
- S:CE by nature takes a strike, which means that you may only play 1 per round
and you cannot hit the opposing minion with that strike. Now, Skin of Rock
does not require a strike, can be played as much as needed during combat, and
you can still hit the opposing minion with a strike. So it seems that Skin of
Rock is a better card. Therefore, if Majesty costs 1 blood, Skin of Rock must
also cost 1 blood. This is how the "balance" is created for this game. There
must be a better way.

>>It'll also unwallpaper Staredown. If Majesty costs a blood, I'll be packing
my Presence decks with a whole lot of Staredowns and a handful of
Majesty/Catatonic Fear from now on.

Yeah, it's true, Staredown is a wallpaper card - bringing Majesty down to its
wallpaper level isn't fun. I think staredown has it's purpose - it's a
presence dodge - which is cool for Toreadors with guns. However, it is still
not a good S:CE card. Making the rest of the S:CE cards also not good destroys
a whole strategy of the game.

>>So far as I can see, rules are not changed to "appease" people. Whenever I
have corresponded with LSJ regarding rulings or rules changes where I have had
a problem with a specific section of the set-up, very

little has been weighed in the balance of "appeasing" people. People "crying"

has never resulted in action being taken that I have ever seen. People
presenting logical, thoughtful, well-planned, well- argued points of view,
backed up with theory and practise in multiple situations, has resulted in
action being taken - not all of which I necessarily agree with entirely, but
corrective action nonetheless.

Well thought out complaints are still complaints. Sure, crying is a harsh
word, but I believe that many of the reworded cards have been reworded from
constant bitching from people who have felt "abused" by them.

>>Toning down doing little for balancing is a different issue, however. First
of all, it is necessary to demonstrate that different elements are "toned
down", and that they haven't advanced since through new cards. Second of all,
it is necessary to demonstrate that toning down doesn't
balance the game.

Toning down a game's elements does bring some balance to a game - but never
will all cards be equal. Toning up a game elements does bring the same balance
as toning down (you tone up weaker strategies to equal stronger ones.) Of
course the cards will still never be equal, but I really don't see how S:CE is
abusive. Only broken cards need to be toned down. Strategy balances should be
done with rules changes.

>>You are one group. One group is welcome, on its own, to do whatever it
wants.

So, I have to play with myself now? That's fine with me - How about I not play
at all? I have obviously been playing wrong for many years now - having fun
with majesty. I guess all those fun times were wrong.

>>Burning vampires is not the same as a measure of balance. Just because it
would be easier to burn vampires under your proposed change, this does not make
it a useful measure of balance. You have not demonstrated that burning
vampires is necessary. You have not demonstrated that combat is underpowered.
You have not demonstrated that combat will benefit from being upgraded in such
a fashion, without detriment. (For instance, whilst one type of aggravated
damage deck might remain balanced under your proposed change, there may be
others which do not.)

I simply think that the rule is a fun simple one. I think it adds to the
excitement of the game. I don't think combat decks need boosting. But then
why would they change S:CE? (rumor of course) How is making vampires nearly
impossible to burn balanced? Rules effect the balance of the game, but no rule
can outbalance another rule - only cards can be balanced, (and perhaps
strategies)

>>This is based on the premise that S:CE has been wallpapered. There is no
evidence to suggest from where I stand that S:CE has been wallpapered. "Then
why wallpaper S:CE" is an excellent sound-bite. But you need to put in a lot
of work to show that it's been wallpapered. There are certain specific sources
of Strike: Combat Ends which may have been addressed, or may be addressed in
the Camarilla Edition (about which I have no knowledge other than the vague
rumours circulating), but other sources of S:CE have been introduced at the
same time.

The wallpapering of S:CE is at this point a rumor of course. I wish that White
Wolf would make a full disclosure, so that we could discuss such matters -
because they pertain to the discussions of the overall changes of the set.
However, I have a feeling that WW is trying to diffuse these discussions as
much as possible. But to say there is NO evidence is asinine. The rumor
exists, and I believe it came from an unofficial spoiler, also WW has an
upcoming section on the preview about card changes.

This thread (hopefully) shows that there are ways to balance a game besides
wallpapering cards. I just thought it would be good to get people thinking
about what balance means before the official information about card changes
comes out. Do we need to implement this rule change? No. Would it help the
game? Maybe or maybe not. Do we need to wallpaper majesty? No. Would it
help the game or make people quit? This remains to be seen.

Anyway, I'd like to be done with this thread. We could go on and on about
balance and how rules changes effect cards - but it really doesn't matter,
because WW seems to be only concerned with bringing in new players - it doesn't
matter what we think.

In message <20020721022039...@mb-fk.aol.com>, Awazzzz
<awa...@aol.com> writes:

*PLEASE* respect Usenet etiquette.

1) Putting two replies in the same post is *wrong*.
2) Following up to the wrong posts is *wrong*.
3) Not citing the people to whom you are replying, especially when there
are several sections of material in the same post from entirely
different responses is *wrong*.

*PLEASE* learn how to drive your news-reader properly. If your news-
reader isn't up to the task, get a better one.

If you want people to respond to your posts with reasoned responses, you
need to put in work so that other people can follow what you're replying
to, from whom. The idea is to make things easy for everyone else to
read, by your putting in a few seconds more work. (Hitting follow-up to
a separate post is not hard.)

Having to fight with your posts to work out what's from where is *not* a
good way to get people to take your arguments seriously. You really
need to make things as easy as possible for the reader.

>>>So far as I can see, rules are not changed to "appease" people. Whenever I
>have corresponded with LSJ regarding rulings or rules changes where I have had
>a problem with a specific section of the set-up, very
>little has been weighed in the balance of "appeasing" people. People "crying"
>has never resulted in action being taken that I have ever seen. People
>presenting logical, thoughtful, well-planned, well- argued points of view,
>backed up with theory and practise in multiple situations, has resulted in
>action being taken - not all of which I necessarily agree with entirely, but
>corrective action nonetheless.
>
>Well thought out complaints are still complaints.

So?

Complaints that have a thought-out purposes, backed up by facts, are
*also* convincing arguments.

That's what's needed to bring about change. Convincing arguments,
combining theory and practise, together with suitable remedial
possibilities for balance.

>>>Toning down doing little for balancing is a different issue, however. First
>of all, it is necessary to demonstrate that different elements are "toned
>down", and that they haven't advanced since through new cards. Second of all,
>it is necessary to demonstrate that toning down doesn't
>balance the game.
>
>Toning down a game's elements does bring some balance to a game - but never
>will all cards be equal.

No, this is a given.

However, you now contradict yourself. Previously, you have stated
categorically that toning down rules brings only a little balance to the
game.

Now you state that it can bring some balance to the game.

Contradictions a go-go.

>Toning up a game elements does bring the same balance
>as toning down (you tone up weaker strategies to equal stronger ones.) Of
>course the cards will still never be equal, but I really don't see how S:CE is
>abusive. Only broken cards need to be toned down. Strategy balances should be
>done with rules changes.

You haven't demonstrated that S:CE is abusive.

You haven't shown that S:CE is being toned down.

There is a rumour that one specific source of S:CE is being adjusted.
This is rebalancing a card.

You have also previously stated that:

"Balance has to do with cards in a game, not the rules of it."

Now you are stating that balance of specific sections of the game
(strategy related) is done with the rules.

Sitting down and thinking through what you're writing would probably aid
you in avoiding such obvious contradictions.

>>>You are one group. One group is welcome, on its own, to do whatever it
>wants.
>
>So, I have to play with myself now?

Erm, no. One group. See?

However, one group will always be atypical.

Is everyone else supposed to play by your rules?

Rules changes are made for the good of the entire game. Different
tournaments need to have a generally balanced rules set-up, as do all
games played by such rules.

If you want to tone up combat because your group plays it a lot more, or
a lot less, or whatever, that's fine. Some tournaments already do this
- specifically twisting rules to reflect a specific balance they want.
Clan only decks, combative decks, alternative rules and so on.

This is separate, however, from game balance as a whole.

Combat is *not* the only facet of the game. The game was principally
designed with three active strategies, with some hybridisation being
expected in the stronger decks. (Others have emerged since, with new
cards and new clans. Lock down, in the form of Ravnos denial, is new.
Corruption is mostly new, though combat/Graverobbing could achieve
something analogous.)

Vote decks still need to be balanced against combat decks. Vote/rush
hybrid decks - a pretty fearsome combination when it works, as it can -
still need to be balanced. Bleed decks still need to be balanced
against combat decks. Bruise and bleed still needs to be balanced.

You have stated yourself, quite clearly:

"I personally do not think combat decks are underpowered."

However, you are now arguing for combat decks to be empowered.
(Bizarre, but true.)

Please demonstrate that upgrading combat decks - which are "not
underpowered" (your words) - will not break them, and will not break
balance between them and other popular, standard archetypes, as designed
into the game.

>That's fine with me - How about I not play
>at all? I have obviously been playing wrong for many years now - having fun
>with majesty. I guess all those fun times were wrong.

*sigh*

Majesty is at the top end of the power curve. This is pretty difficult
to argue against. A basic set aims to provide a balanced, so far as is
possible, set for new players to begin with. This provides a useful
opportunity for rebalancing cards which are seriously out of alignment.

That is all.

This is not a question of "fun". This is a question of balancing cards,
so that cost (which includes many factors - clan, discipline, age,
blood, cost in hand, cost in library etc.), opportunity cost (generally
significant enough to separate it from cost per se) and effect are all
roughly balanced, in the grand scheme of things.

>>>Burning vampires is not the same as a measure of balance. Just because it
>would be easier to burn vampires under your proposed change, this does not make
>it a useful measure of balance. You have not demonstrated that burning
>vampires is necessary. You have not demonstrated that combat is underpowered.
>You have not demonstrated that combat will benefit from being upgraded in such
>a fashion, without detriment. (For instance, whilst one type of aggravated
>damage deck might remain balanced under your proposed change, there may be
>others which do not.)
>
>I simply think that the rule is a fun simple one.

Simplicity is not the only measure of utility.

The rule *MUST* still be balanced, when finished. (If you don't want a
balanced game, that's separate. However, Jyhad has been designed from
the start to be balanced. Mistakes have been made, and rectified.)

You stated:

"Since the old rule is more balanced,
can we reinstate it?"

Since balance is one of the key criteria for rules changes, you need to
demonstrate what you have stated - that the "old rule is more balanced".

Rules being "fun" and "simple" are not usually useful arguments for
radical balance shifts. "Fun" and "simple" may, however, be extremely
useful arguments where multiple options present themselves; picking the
"simple" remedy may then be best, or whatever.

However, before a change can be made, you need to demonstrate that the
game, cards, archetypes and decks will still be balanced, after the
change.

You have already stated that "the old rule is more balanced". Please
provide proof that "the old rule is more balanced", not more soundbites.

>I think it adds to the
>excitement of the game. I don't think combat decks need boosting.

Then don't boost them.

>But then
>why would they change S:CE? (rumor of course)

The only rumour I have heard is a change to Majesty. This is not the
same as changing S:CE. The change to Majesty is also a fairly minor
one, which will still leave the card to be eminently useful, played
sensibly. Attempting to play any card, post-change, as it was played
pre-change, without re-examining it and adjusting as necessary is likely
to result in failure. This is not the same as the card being wallpaper
or unplayable, of course.

If you have heard other, specific, rumours regarding S:CE, bring them
forward.

Affecting one source of S:CE is not the same as changing S:CE. Please
learn the difference.

>How is making vampires nearly
>impossible to burn balanced?

"Making"? The situation that currently exists is already here.

You have stated, repeatedly, that "I don't think combat decks need
boosting." If combat decks don't need boosting, it follows that they
are (roughly, within the limits possible) balanced. (Or, potentially,
overly powerful - if they don't need to be boosted, because they're
already too good. However, we can leave this possibility to one side.)

It is also likely to be true that it is not "nearly impossible" to burn
vampires.

I regularly see vampires being burned. Anathema is an extremely good
card for such, for example. Similarly, dealing multiple points of
aggravated damage, or sufficient regular damage to wound a vampire,
combined with a point of aggravated damage is certainly possible.

For example:

- A Gangrel deck can generate additional damage, in order to create a
wounded vampire, using Ritual Challenge (potentially slow,
though Freak Drive speeds it up usefully), Gangrel Revel
(expensive and fragile), Carrion Crows (for my money, one of the
best cards in the game), Strength of the Bear (well balanced and
useful, at fall-back, enough to include in decks with no, or
only a little, Spiritus, especially with its stackability),
Blissful Agony/Scorpion Sting and so on. Retainers are,
generally, a poor option, though again Freak Drive can speed
things up usefully.

Going in combat with ANI/pro Gangrel (doable at five capacity) and even
ani/pro Gangrel (doable at three capacity, with Anastasia Grey) can then
allow:

- Pre-range - Carrion Crows
- Strength of the Bear
- Range - Quick Meld (maybe)
- Strike - Scorpion Sting
- Strike-modifier - Claws of the Dead

With an ANI/pro vampires, that's 5 damage, three of which is aggravated,
coming from two different sources (thus harder for Skin of Steel), some
of which is (obviously) environmental, some of which is aggravated (thus
making some of the damage prevention sources unusable, specifically pro-
based Flesh of Marble, but a few others exist).

Cost? Five cards, two blood. All five are useful cards. Quick Meld
may well not even be necessary, metagame-willing.

You hit, you can burn a vampire, or torporise them.

Similarly, you can throw down Amaranth. Difficult for the Gangrel, but
a well-tuned deck may be including Stansylvania, a very useful vampire,
or Gangrel Justicar (either Gangrel Justicar, the vote card, or Angus
the Unruled, or whoever the new Gangrel Justicar will be in the
Camarilla Edition) and fiddle with Absolution of the Diabolist. This is
playable during your minion phase, by specific card text.

The Gangrel Antitribu have many of the tactics of the Gangrel available
to them, for the Country Gangrel. The Country Gangrel also have Gangrel
Conspiracy available to them. (Again, playable during your own turn.)

The City Gangrel Antitribu (obf/cel/pro) have different discipline
splits, and thus some of the cards available aren't useful. However,
Celerity provides for additional strikes. Both Gangrel and !Gangrel can
access Shadow of the Wolf, though it's probably a poor choice for the
!Gangrel - a Blur might be better. However, again, a single point of
aggravated damage (unprevented), Amaranth, Gangrel Conspiracy is a
perfectly usable combo. (Slow, due to the M:OOT restrictions of one per
turn, but doable.)

These are all useful combinations, but with restrictions stopping them
being easy. *No* strategy is supposed to "just happen" - costing should
make them expensive, relative to their output, and interaction should be
possible at many levels.

- The Tzimisce can use a number of the Animalism tricks of the Gangrel,
above. Vicissitude helps replace some of the tricks of Protean. For
instance, Chiropteran Marauder helps replace the claw. Body Arsenal and
Horrid Form are also useful substitutes. They lose out slightly on
maneuvers, but gain in assorted other ways - War Ghoul is often a better
bet than Renegade Garou, even with his cigar.

Combining Carrion Crows (I really cannot emphasise how useful this card
is), Strength of the Bear (Dragos would have fun with it, if he didn't
already have 'vic' which more or less works out the same with its combat
modifiers), a source of aggravated damage, a source of additional hand
damage e.g. Scorpion Sting, is all very easy, for a small investment in
cards. Flinging Amaranth is possible, but not the best of options -
their votes are quite expensive, a 6 bishop, 8, 8, 9, 10. Diplomacy and
negotiation may allow diablerie to be explored, which is certainly
doable. The Gangrel and Country !Gan also have Freak Drive, allowing
rush/freak/diablerie, all with one vampire.

- Any potence oriented deck has a number of useful cards at its
disposal. Immortal Grapple, Torn Signpost, Increased Strength and
Undead Strength can form the basis of a formidable strike - obviously,
you may only need to play a couple, for any given vampire.

If combined with celerity (principally Brujah and !Bru), additional
strikes can be achieved, which help whittle down damage prevention. If
combined with Obtenebration (Lasombra), there are various interesting
options - Arms of the Abyss is quite popular (though watch out for IG
conflicts). If combined with Protean, many options can be explored, but
this is an expensive route (thus achieving a measure of balance).
Obfuscate has provided a nice set of options in the past - obf/pot is a
*very* small investment, capacity-wise. A search through Google's
archives will reveal some of the absolutely scary average capacities
that have been achieved, where it almost feels like you're getting pool
to play those vampires. It falls down to Skin of Steel (where Celerity
needs superior Skin of Steel, or similar), but it's a viable option,
especially if it's combat/something combined. If you're playing
Nosferatu or !Nos, you could even drop in a few Animalism cards, for
Carrion Crows, which helps combat that tendencies.

Potence, however, then brings in some other fantastic options.
Diablerie, via Amaranth or separate actions, is always possible. But
Potence has two extremely useful cards - Disarm and Decapitate. Blood
won't save you, if enough damage is done (which only needs to be more
than the other person) - you go to torpor. Then you burn. Immortal
Grapple, Undead Strength, Disarm, Decapitate - four cards, 2 blood,
burned vampire. Just requires POT, which is relatively simple to access
- four caps, for CEL/POT (Jimmy Dunn) and obf/POT (Agatha), as well as a
few other vamps, less directly combative.

It follows that claiming that it is nearly impossible to burn vampires
is hard to support.

Could you provide proof of your "nearly impossible" claim, rather than a
soundbite?

>Rules effect the balance of the game, but no rule
>can outbalance another rule - only cards can be balanced, (and perhaps
>strategies)

This is a curious assertion. Rules define the templates within which
cards work. Cards and rules together create strategies.

The idea is that, at the end of the day, each item created by rules
should be balanced. For instance, dropping the Bloodhunt rule willy-
nilly would unbalance certain facets of the game. (As well as
wallpapering a few cards, but that's separate.)

Rules create and sustain balance, in tandem with cards, within the game
as a whole.

You have not demonstrated that combat is negatively unbalanced (i.e.
underpowered). Indeed, you have claimed that it isn't.

You have not demonstrated that upgrading the aggravated damage rules
away from the current template (which is close to Jyhad costing and
balance) will not unbalance these facets of the game.

You have not demonstrated many things. Please provide proof, not
soundbites.

>>>This is based on the premise that S:CE has been wallpapered. There is no

Please provide direct details of the rumour. Such issues can then be

>Wolf would make a full disclosure, so that we could discuss such matters -
>because they pertain to the discussions of the overall changes of the set.
>However, I have a feeling that WW is trying to diffuse these discussions as

The rumours exist that Majesty may be costed. (Potentially also
Catatonic Fear.)

This is not the same as S:CE being wallpapered.

If you have specific rumours to address, please address them.

However, rumours and speculation are not evidence.

>This thread (hopefully) shows that there are ways to balance a game besides
>wallpapering cards.

You've shown *nothing*. Honestly. You've *SHOWN* nothing.

You haven't provided proof. You haven't cited current winning decks.
You haven't explored avenues for balance. You haven't explored designer
intent. You have made many repeated errors.

You haven't provided anything other than items like:

- combat should be upgraded because I like it
- it would be "fun" and "simple"
- confusing items like "simple" and "balanced" interchangeably

and so on.

If you want to *SHOW* something, do it. Sit down, work it through,
provide examples, provide theories, provide practise, provide
speculation if you want.

But actually *SHOW* something.

You haven't shown that any specific cards are being wallpapered, either.

>Anyway, I'd like to be done with this thread. We could go on and on about
>balance and how rules changes effect cards - but it really doesn't matter,
>because WW seems to be only concerned with bringing in new players - it doesn't
>matter what we think.

Before you're done with the thread, would it be possible for you to stop
providing soundbites about cards being wallpapered and actually provide
some solid, workable *EVIDENCE* and *PROOF* for those soundbites?

If all you say is "S:CE is being wallpapered" without backing it up with
*proof*, you don't advance anything.

If you want to advance things in a useful way, actually back up your
assertions, rather than coming up with more soundbites about "fun",
"simple", "balanced" and "wallpaper", without providing any actual basis
in pan-game fact for them.

If you don't provide proof for the need for a change, nothing's going to
change. Assuming you *want* the changes, you need to prove why they're
needed. And if you can provide useful, solid proof, that works in
useful, thematic, theoretic, practical, pan-game, pan-strategy ways,
rather than a focus of "I like burning vampires, ergo...", you'll garner
some support. Indeed, if you can provide useful, solid proof of that
sort for your arguments, I'll support it myself.

Oh, cripes! I dislike having arguments about minor Usenet netiquette
points but I dislike people making pretentious claims that about "rules"
that just aren't so even more. At best these come down as readability
recommendations that can sometimes even be counterproductive if followed
rigidly. I will include replies to multiple posts in a single post
at times when I think it's reasonable and efficient to respond to various
posts that way. And nothing you say will ever make me stop that because
it's a stupid concept as an all-inclusive "rule". Following-up a single
post using the wrong previous post reference is weird and defeats a minor
feature of threaded newsreaders but - particularly when done in the correct
thread at least - is not a serious problem. Only your third point, about
citing the author of quoted text accurately and in a non-confusing way,
causes real problems.

> 3) Not citing the people to whom you are replying, especially when there
> are several sections of material in the same post from entirely
> different responses is *wrong*.

What it comes down to is common sense. To make your posts as readable as
possible and to avoid causing confusion (which can sometimes blossom into
full-scale anger and loathing), quote text you're responding to, quote it
in a way that we can separate what you're quoting and what you're saying in
response, cite the author of the quoted text accurately and understandably,
don't quote unnecessary text, and put your response where we can see what
it responds to - meaning underneath the appropriate quote and not on top
of it.

All of these things are just minor writing style issues which are not
particularly important if we can understand the author's meaning well enough
in spite of such transgressions. There's no need to constantly harp on
them. It's only when someone habitually pumps out posts that cause serious
confusion. FOR INSTANCE: if someone finds it necessary to post in order to
ask the author for clarification of what he meant to say or if a flame-war
starts due to confusion about who said what, then something is seriously
wrong. If something like that happens, then it might be worth posting to
_suggest_ some common sense rules to avoid problems.

Fred

>Oh, cripes! I dislike having arguments about minor Usenet netiquette
>points but I dislike people making pretentious claims that about "rules"
>that just aren't so even more.

Would you care to cite current examples of best practise where the
References: line doesn't work how it has always worked?

The References: line exists for a *specific* reason - that of threading.
The idea is to construct threads, not just post after post after post,
like on a web-based forum.

Even Google can cope with threading.

Threads also allow people to isolate what's being referred to, easily.
You can back up to the previous post to see what was said, in a wider
context, assuming you have the post, since in a thread of a hundred
articles the previous article may have been read 50 posts ago.

It's how Usenet *works*. Threading is fundamental to Usenet. USEFOR's
current drafts reinforces this. USER represents, in many respects,
current best practice (there are some areas where it defines new
practice, of course); arguing that is just isn't so is wilfully ignoring
the facts.

I am sorry if citing Usenet mechanisms, practise and drafts for the
future is "pretentious".

If you don't want a threaded medium, using Usenet is probably a bad
idea. Whilst using Usenet, however, respecting its threaded nature is
probably best and most useful. It's how Usenet works, it's how people
will expect it to work. If you don't like the facts of how Usenet
works, there's not a lot I can do about that.
