In message <20020723011030...@mb-mp.aol.com>, Awazzzz

<awa...@aol.com> writes:
>Josh, it certainly is easier to burn vamps with an ivory bow with the V:TES
>rule, because with the current rule, it is impossible to burn a vamp with just
>an Ivory Bow.

Correct. When Ivory Bow was designed, it was impossible to burn a
vampire with just an Ivory Bow.

Irrespective of anything else in combat, the first aggravated point of
any packet of damage torporised a vampire. As such, it was utterly
impossible to *ever* burn a vampire using an Ivory Bow - the aggravated
damage just couldn't burn them, ever.

This is how the card was designed.

Under current rules, you can combine the Ivory Bow with, say, a source
of environmental damage. For instance, a Wolf Companion style retainer
(there are an assortment of them).

>However, I still wouldn't call it just plain easy. The opposing
>vampire must be at 0 blood, the damage cannot be dodged or prevented, and the
>opposing minion cannot gain any blood, or the vamp does not burn.

The card was balanced, cost-wise, with it being impossible to burn
vampires. It can burn vampires, currently, under a difficult set of
circumstances, and is still a good card.

Why does it need to be made even better?

>You say the
>Ivory Bow is undercosted. It costs 1 pool, where both Society of Leopold and
>Anathems do not cost any pool, and can burn vamps without ever getting into
>combat. Does this mean that we need to wallpaper Society of Leopold and
>Anathema?

You misunderstand how costing works. You also misunderstand how
Anathema works.

Cost
----

Costing is a combination of *many* factors. Simple pool and blood costs
are not the only cost.

For example, a minion card may cost 1 pool. Let's take a Vial of Elder
Vitae as an example - a card which is playable, without being generally
massive.

Vial of Elder Vitae takes up 1 slot in your library and 1 slot in your
hand before you play it, if you draw it. You may then discard it, or
play it. These are pretty much constants across all cards. They form
the base of inherent cost. Practically every card has that. Burn
Option cards in Bloodlines have a reduced cost in terms of time in hand
and discarding - that's what makes them cheaper and more attractive,
since they don't take up the same space as standard cards, so if you
don't get your scarce bloodline vampire out, you can throw the card very
quickly. (Of course, overloading on them will still slow you down,
especially if you *do* get the vampire out.)

A card may then be costed additionally to 1 pool. It might require a
specific clan. This requires having members of a specific clan out,
which restricts its use, or makes it more lucky (for instance, in cross-
clan decks).

For instance, Patronage may be regarded as roughly similar to Vial of
Elder Vitae. They both take one action to bring out, and both have
transient effects. True, Vial of Elder Vitae's can be kept for later,
but it can also be stolen or destroyed (though such things tend to
happen by accident, rather than a deck necessarily planning for stealing
equipment, unless a meta-game shifts heavily). But Patronage gives you
an extra action, which can be fiendishly powerful. A deck may plan
around "Well, he's got four vampires, I can block three of the bleeds,
and even if it has one last vote I can cope" - and then suddenly find
itself with five vampires to deal with. Extra actions are powerful. So
the card is restricted with a clan restriction, making it harder to use.
It is *also* restricted with an age restriction - you need two vampires
out (so a combat deck can cause you problems) and one of them needs to
be older than the other (less problematic, if you have two out, nine
times out of ten). And is only playable once per turn.

The effect is powerful, but the cost becomes more than just the pool
cost, and so the card is roughly balanced.

Other similar and varied costs may be employed. For instance, if we
look at Treasured Samadji, that's a similar card. 1 pool, equipment.
Permanent effect - unlike Vial of Elder Vitae which needs to be burned.
However, it's unique (unlike Vial of Elder Vitae, which can be played
multiple times) and requires a clan.

Anything that requires a vote means you have to bring out lots of vote
related resources to pass the vote, or face problems as people vote it
down if its not in their interests. Sure, diplomacy is possible - but
it's not a guarantee. If your prey is playing the *other* vote deck,
it's difficult - they're not going to support you. You have to bring
out voting vampires, you have to bring out vote locations (Ventrue HQ
and similar), or pack your deck with vote related cards (Awe, Bewitching
Oration, whatever), or have lots of goodies to offer other people
("Support this and I'll...") which weakens your deck focus and so on.

Master cards work differently. Each card competes for a very limited
resource - master phase actions. These are generally in short supply,
though an end-game may result in many short, fast turns, as players
cautiously advance, leaving defences untapped. The Parthenon is
expensive, as are other resources - Anson, Rumours of Gehenna, and so
on.

Cards compete for master card slots, so can only be played one per turn.
Different power levels can be established, as a result, because of this
different cost. Clan requirements, uniqueness, pool costs, whatever -
they can all be employed too.

Anathema
--------

Anathema is very specifically combat related. They need to be *in
combat* to burn. As a result, your deck will need to be able to survive
at least one combat. This is as a specific result of Anathema's card
text. As a result, a dedicated combat deck should be able to beat you
(because you are having to devote some time to the vote, whilst he is
having to devote all his time to the combat), and a lot of combat
defence should be able to stall you. (It might not stall other players,
who get an advantage, but if the targeted vampire dies, you get some
advantage anyway.)

One possible option, which I've never seen explored, goes as
follows, however. Call Anathema (needs a Prince or Justicar). Call
Free States Rant (needs an independent vampire). You can kill a vampire
outside of combat. *Then* you go into one combat, and ping them there.

Matt Green has done some sterling work in the past with Gratiano and
Lucita. The idea of bringing out Gratiano - because his additional vote
would work in the sub-referendum, thus guaranteeing a Priscus vote for
three, which is a lot in the Free States Rant referendum, which throws
everything to cock - and using Lucita to call the Free States Rant vote
is well understood.

If we bring out Lucita, Gratiano and Marcus Vitel, using Marcus for his
Praxis and Fifth Tradition: Horse Brutality/Minion Tap, even if it does
get downgraded. Assuming they don't Majesty/Earth Meld/whatever
(Immortal Grapple), you can thrown down Darkness Within. And you can
get more pool back from the Anathema, to pay for whoever. Hmm....

Anathema is, however, balanced by a number of factors. First of all,
it's a vote. Then it needs to be called by a Prince or Justicar - if
you can take down that/those Prince(s) or Justicar(s), the vote simply
cannot be called. Then the vote needs to pass - if you can play
Delaying Tactics, that buggers them for a turn, if you're playing a vote
deck, you're going to make life difficult by failing the vote or they're
going to have to *really* work to pass it (and remember, they may well
be playing some combat in the deck too, so every vote card becomes that
little bit harder to get). Then they need to enter combat with that
vampire (and even a Rush deck can benefit from the odd Wake or two),
which might hard - though they may be using Archon, since they have
Princes and Justicars, but then that competes for even more vote
tactics. (A few Havens or Bum's Rushes or whatever are likely to still
be in such a deck.) Then they have to get you down to zero blood, which
may be difficult if you're playing cannily, and have some defence
available - Majesty (if you have more than one blood, or it could burn
you), Ex Nihilo (difficult), Skin of Rock/Skin of Steel (escapable by
using Theft of Vitae or something, but a Tremere vote/rush deck would be
difficult, similarly the Assamites would have trouble). And they can
still fight back, if they're a combat deck. If you go in to burn them,
they can still throw Torn Signposts back at you. Or Horrid Forms. Or
.44 Magnums (and then you need to hit them at range) - even better with
Concealed Weapon. Or... there are lots of possibilities.

And lots of decks are mindful of combat, either actively or defensively,
which means it isn't just a walk in the park.

No, a combat deck doesn't hold all the aces against Anathema. But
Anathema doesn't hold all the aces against a combat deck. They're not
supposed to.

They're *supposed* to be balanced against one another. And you've
stated that combat decks don't need to upgraded, so one assumes that
they're roughly balanced. Combat decks get a lot of secondary resource
ability. Bleed decks get a lot of primary resource ability. Vote decks
can straddle the two, as their composition dictates, but since both
primary and secondary resource manipulation will need the same back-up
for a vote deck - that of vote passing - but the actual referendum will
only need one card, combining heavy primary resource manipulation
(Parity Shift, Autarkis Persecution, Ancilla Empowerment, Consanguineous
Boon, Kine Resources Contested - that sort of card) with minor secondary
resource manipulation (Banishment, Free States Rant (potentially),
Sacrifice (ow, my eyes, Derange, ow, ow), Protect Thine Own, Peace
Treaty, Disputed Territory), together with some of the just plain screwy
vote cards (Kindred Restructure, say) gives it a lot of flexibility.

I can't think of a neater way to balance such a game. It's extremely
neatly done, as far back as Jyhad - though they didn't predict that
combat defence would be quite so prominent with multiple Majesty or
multiple Earth Meld (the primary sources of S:CE at the time). But
that's been rectified neatly since, with many forms of combat empowering
cards.

>No, a simple rule change could restore much balance.

You haven't demonstrated that balance is missing, to be restored.

You have stated: "I personally do not think combat decks are
underpowered."

This is the very antithesis of what you are arguing. You are arguing
that they need to be balanced up, when they aren't underpowered.

You have demonstrated that the current rule makes burning vampires
harder to do. This is a given, that's what it's designed to do. You
haven't demonstrated:

- that having vampires harder to burn unbalances combat strategies to be
underpowered. You have stated that you "do not think combat
decks are underpowered", which is the reverse of this proof.

- that re-arranging the aggravated damage rules in the manner you
suggest won't break them. Ivory Bow was designed so that it
couldn't burn things on its own, which it still can't.
Starshell Grenade Launcher was designed with the current rules-
set. Improvised Flamethrower was designed with the current
rules-set. True Faith was designed with the current rules-set.
Sword of the Righteous was designed with the current rules-set.
Elemental Stoicism was designed with the current rules-set.
Domain of Evernight was designed with the current rules-set.
Conflagration was designed with the current rules-set.
Concordance was designed with the current rules set. Compress
was designed with the current rules-set. Armor of Terra was
designed with the current rules-set. Mythic Form was designed
with the current rules-set. Ex Nihilo was designed with the
current rules set. Masquer was designed with the current rules
set.

Are you sure that those cards weren't costed, designed, tested and
balanced knowing what the current rules set is, and compensating for it
in their design?

I ask you again: Demonstrate that the current rules set *needs* to be
balanced in the fashion you suggest. Demonstrate that balance is
missing. Just that burning vampires takes time and effort is not
indicative of imbalance, when that's what the rules have been designed

But it looks to me like balance already exists. Society of Leopold
and Anathema have their own compensating drawbacks: Society will
only burn an empty vampire if played while it's empty; otherwise it
just burns one blood each turn and the card might get moved to
another vampire (quite possibly one of your own vamps). Anathema
requires passing a vote, and then to burn a vampire you also have
to reduce the Anathematized vamp to 0 blood in combat.

Ivory Bow, once in play, lets you send vamps to torpor (which
generally costs them 2 blood) each time you get in combat, and
the possibility of burning empty vamps will exist for the entire
game.

Aggravated damage is by no means weak with the current agg damage
rules. As such, I see no reason to change it.

>>When Ivory Bow was designed, it was impossible to burn a vampire with just an
Ivory Bow. Irrespective of anything else in combat, the first aggravated point
of any packet of damage torporised a vampire. As such, it was utterly
impossible to *ever* burn a vampire using an Ivory Bow - the aggravated
damage just couldn't burn them, ever. This is how the card was designed.
Under current rules, you can combine the Ivory Bow with, say, a source of
environmental damage. For instance, a Wolf Companion style retainer (there are

an assortment of them). The card was balanced, cost-wise, with it being

impossible to burn vampires. It can burn vampires, currently, under a
difficult set of circumstances, and is still a good card. Why does it need to
be made even better?

It is not just Ivory Bow that will be made better by the proposed rule change,
but all cards with agg damage. These cards, as you say, can burn vampires
under a difficult set of circumstances. But, I am not sure the set of
circumstances described would actually burn a vampire. The environmental
damage would be normal damage - it does not become agg. You need 2 points of
agg to burn a vampire, therefore under these circumstances it is still not
possible to burn an opposing minion with an Ivory Bow. Still, with the right
cards - it should still be possible - ivory bow, ghoul retainer, starshell
grenede launcher. All together this combo costs 5 pool. Anathema does not
cost any pool.

>>You misunderstand how costing works. You also misunderstand how Anathema
works.

>>Cost - Costing is a combination of *many* factors. Simple pool and blood

costs
are not the only cost. For example, a minion card may cost 1 pool. Let's take
a Vial of Elder
Vitae as an example - a card which is playable, without being generally
massive. Vial of Elder Vitae takes up 1 slot in your library and 1 slot in
your hand before you play it, if you draw it. You may then discard it, or play
it. These are pretty much constants across all cards. They form the base of
inherent cost. Practically every card has that. Burn Option cards in
Bloodlines have a reduced cost in terms of time in hand and discarding - that's
what makes them cheaper and more attractive, since they don't take up the same
space as standard cards, so if you don't get your scarce bloodline vampire out,
you can throw the card very quickly. (Of course, overloading on them will
still slow you down, especially if you *do* get the vampire out.)

James, you are right, all non-burn-option cards have this cost. Therefore it
creates no balance issue.

>>A card may then be costed additionally to 1 pool.

Or more than 1 pool.

>>It might require a specific clan. This requires having members of a specific
clan out, which restricts its use, or makes it more lucky (for instance, in

cross-clan decks). For instance, Patronage may be regarded as roughly similar

to Vial of Elder Vitae. They both take one action to bring out, and both have
transient effects. True, Vial of Elder Vitae's can be kept for later, but it
can also be stolen or destroyed (though such things tend to happen by accident,
rather than a deck necessarily planning for stealing equipment, unless a
meta-game shifts heavily). But Patronage gives you an extra action, which can
be fiendishly powerful. A deck may plan around "Well, he's got four vampires,
I can block three of the bleeds, and even if it has one last vote I can cope" -
and then suddenly find itself with five vampires to deal with. Extra actions
are powerful. So the card is restricted with a clan restriction, making it
harder to use. It is *also* restricted with an age restriction - you need two
vampires out (so a combat deck can cause you problems) and one of them needs to
be older than the other (less problematic, if you have two out, nine times out
of ten). And is only playable once per turn. The effect is powerful, but the
cost becomes more than just the pool
cost, and so the card is roughly balanced. Other similar and varied costs may
be employed.

James, of course there are other costs besides pool costs. The Ivory Bow has
costs beyond it's 1 pool. It requires a card slot, it requires an action (or
another card) to bring into play, combat must occur, other cards must be added
to it for it to burn a vampire.

>>Anathema is very specifically combat related. They need to be *in combat* to
burn. As a result, your deck will need to be able to survive at least one
combat. This is as a specific result of Anathema's card
text. As a result, a dedicated combat deck should be able to beat you (because
you are having to devote some time to the vote, whilst he is having to devote
all his time to the combat), and a lot of combat
defence should be able to stall you. (It might not stall other players, who
get an advantage, but if the targeted vampire dies, you get some advantage
anyway.)

When you build a deck, you make sure you can provide all the necessary
requirements for playing the cards in it. I personally like the Euro-Brujah
for Anathema. With Anathema one also gains pool to the vampire's capacity.
While it is not guaranteed that the person playing anathema is going to get
this pool, their deck will probably be designed to attempt to get it. Maybe
someone is playing with a better combat deck than yours, maybe not. At least
the deck will be prepared to go to combat and gain the pool. You burn a
vampire AND gain pool equal to it's capacity. Ivory Bow has all the same
requirements and costs except for the title and vote. It also has the 1 pool
cost which Anathema does not. It cannot burn vampires or gain pool.

>>No, a combat deck doesn't hold all the aces against Anathema. But Anathema
doesn't hold all the aces against a combat deck. They're not supposed to.
They're *supposed* to be balanced against one another. And you've stated that
combat decks don't need to upgraded, so one assumes that they're roughly
balanced. Combat decks get a lot of secondary resource ability. Bleed decks
get a lot of primary resource ability. Vote decks can straddle the two, as
their composition dictates, but since both primary and secondary resource
manipulation will need the same back-up for a vote deck - that of vote passing
- but the actual referendum will only need one card, combining heavy primary
resource manipulation (Parity Shift, Autarkis Persecution, Ancilla Empowerment,
Consanguineous Boon, Kine Resources Contested - that sort of card) with minor
secondary resource manipulation (Banishment, Free States Rant (potentially),
Sacrifice (ow, my eyes, Derange, ow, ow), Protect Thine Own, Peace Treaty,
Disputed Territory), together with some of the just plain screwy vote cards
(Kindred Restructure, say) gives it a lot of flexibility.

Going after one's secondary resources (vampires) keeps them from going after
their prey's primary resource (pool) . This is why I think that the strategies
are balanced against each other and combat does not need upgrading. However,
decks that attack the secondary resource could be more effective at destroying
the secondary resource without harming this balance. One could still protect
their secondary resources. This is why combat defense and blood gain is
essential to keeping the balance of the strategies.

>>I can't think of a neater way to balance such a game. It's extremely neatly
done, as far back as Jyhad - though they didn't predict that combat defence
would be quite so prominent with multiple Majesty or
multiple Earth Meld (the primary sources of S:CE at the time). But that's been
rectified neatly since, with many forms of combat empowering cards.

V:TES is an extremely balanced game. It is just in the nature of the mechanics
alone. Vampires cost pool and transfers. Playing cards and ousting your prey
requires vampires. It is such a balanced game that it has maintained the NCL
rule, the no-banned policy, and crypt balance. However, some of the cards did
not fit into the balance - they were poorly designed. These cards were
reworded or recosted to fit into the design. But exact balance is never going
to occur. Some cards will always get more tournament play than others.
Majesty is a card that has been a staple card in the game since its inception.
Since it is one of the first cards - it defines what balance is. It's cost and
effect set the pace. It never was out of balance.

>>You haven't demonstrated that balance is missing, to be restored.

They are rebalancing cards - I don't personally think that balance is mising,
but obviously someone does. I think that there must be a better way of
restoring a balance issue than recosting or rewording staple cards.

>>You have stated: "I personally do not think combat decks are underpowered."
This is the very antithesis of what you are arguing. You are arguing that they
need to be balanced up, when they aren't underpowered.

No James, you have obviously not been listening, Combat decks, in my opinion
are not underpowered, and that is not the basis for the proposed rules change.
The basis for the rules change is that adding effect to cards that use agg as
an effect and adding cost to cards that use agg as a cost would balance them
better cost vs. effect when compared with other cards.

>>You have demonstrated that the current rule makes burning vampires harder to
do.

Okay James, whatever

>>You haven't demonstrated: - that having vampires harder to burn unbalances
combat strategies to be underpowered. You have stated that you "do not think
combat decks are underpowered", which is the reverse of this proof. - that
re-arranging the aggravated damage rules in the manner you suggest won't break
them.

I have said that all deck archetypes were still viable when the V:TES rule was
in effect.

>>Ivory Bow was designed so that it couldn't burn things on its own, which it
still can't. Starshell Grenade Launcher was designed with the current

rules-set. Improvised Flamethrower was designed with the current rules-set.

True Faith was designed with the current rules-set. Sword of the Righteous was
designed with the current rules-set. Elemental Stoicism was designed with the
current rules-set. Domain of Evernight was designed with the current
rules-set. Conflagration was designed with the current rules-set. Concordance
was designed with the current rules set. Compress was designed with the
current rules-set. Armor of Terra was designed with the current rules-set.
Mythic Form was designed with the current rules-set. Ex Nihilo was designed
with the current rules set. Masquer was designed with the current rules set.
Are you sure that those cards weren't costed, designed, tested and balanced
knowing what the current rules set is, and compensating for it in their design?

Ahh, finally, someone asks the right question!! Yes, these cards were costed,
designed, tested, and balanced in the current rules set. And yes, changing the
rule would add to the cost or effect of the card the possibility of burning the
vampire, and now that the examples mention it, the possible additional effect
of avoiding said burning. I think it would be a change for the better. It
would add more exitement and drama to the game. And would not deter from the
balance of the game. The possibility that one's vamp might burn from playing
Daring the Dawn, does not take away from it's effect - it does not wallpaper
the card. And while the rule would add to the effect of Ivory Bow without
increasing its cost - the card would still not be broken.

>>I ask you again: Demonstrate that the current rules set *needs* to be
balanced in the fashion you suggest. Demonstrate that balance is missing.
Just that burning vampires takes time and effort is not indicative of
imbalance, when that's what the rules have been designed for.

There are cards that can burn vamps (ie anathema, society of leopold) that can
burn vamps with little cost. Agg damage is never free and cannot burn a vamp
without being added to.

No. However, action cards are not as easily baselined as Master Phase
Actions are. You can only have one MPA a turn, barring a small number
of special effects that change that. There is an MPA that is free and
gains you one pool, and is almost never seen because there are many
other cards that are better. Therefore it makes a suitable baseline;
"how does this card compare to Ascendance?"

Baselining an action is much more complicated, since there could be a
multiple of said actions per turn, and it will be constantly changing.
However, there are a certain number of "default" actions any minion can
take, and baselining against THOSE is perfectly viable: hunt and bleed.
So we can add the baseline for actions and action cards as follows; "how
does this action compare to hunting and/or bleeding for 1?"

In this case, 5th Tradition compares quite favorably to hunting.

>>>Anathema is a political action requiring a Prince/Justicar that must be
>passed as well as called... and unfortunately for you, someone STILL has
>to enter combat with the Anathema'd minion in order to burn it.
>
>That's all true, but not only does one burn a vampire with anathema, they also
>gain pool equal to its capacity. Ivory Bow cannot burn a vampire, cannot gain
>you any pool, and cost 1 pool.

Right, but it's not just the person who called the Anathema who can gain
the pool. That provides a sufficient element of risk to balance (not to
mention the three separate requirements you must meet in order to even
burn an Anathema'd vamp).

>>>Neither Society of Leopold nor Anathema will send vampires to torpor,
>whereas the Ivory Bow will.
>
>This reasoning is so asinine, one might think I said it. Burning a vamp is
>better tha sending it to torpor.

Now, now, Sammy boy, you're missing some very obvious points here.
Burning a vamp may be better than sending it to torpor, but the Ivory
Bow will send to torpor vamps that it CANNOT burn. Society of Leopold
and Anathema will not do this -- meaning that a vamp you target with SoL
or Anathema and don't burn is still around to take actions against you,
or block, or Deflect, or...

It's a very important distinction -- have you played the game recently?

>>>However, the Ivory Bow can be equipped by any minion, including Smudge.
>See the balance?
>
>I can also make smudge a Prince and call anathema.

Requires a Praxis: Seizure card in your deck, and also requires some
means of passing the vote with Smudge -- not quite as easy as you think.

Smudge equipping the Ivory Bow, though, is still only a 1-card cost in
your deck.

>>>Simply put, though, the primary reason to not make vampires easier to
>burn is that it adds that much more risk to playing large vampires. The
>game is already excessively weenie-riffic; we don't need to push it any
>more in that direction.
>
>I agree that the bigger vampires should remain more powerful than the weenines.
> However, a big vamp is less likely to burn than a weenie with this rule,
>because it comes into play with more blood on it.

OK, have you actually tried playing the game against competent people?
Let me break this down to you in words of two syllables:

Amount Of Blood Does Not Matter.

Most combat decks are prepared to knock a full 8-cap into torpor.
(baseline here; Torn Signpost/Blur) While your full 10-cap can survive
it, do you think the 10-cap will remain at full blood the whole game?
No, of course not. You'll be spending that blood or Minion Tapping some
of it back, because NO 10-cap is worth 10 pool. So much for the "lots
of blood = live longer" theory.

The problem is, the 10-cap still takes 10 transfers to bring out... so
even if you manage to Minion Tap some of the pool cost back before it
gets burned, you're still unable to act until you get another target
out.

>>>Consider whether it's worse to get one of five 2-caps burned, or your
>single 10-cap? Right first try. Going back to the V:TES rules simply
>makes it far less worthwhile to even TRY to play with big vamps, because
>the weenie hordes will get you every time.
>
>I played with the V:TES rule during the V:TES days, I was able to play with big
>vamps just fine.

Yeah, but Sam, I don't think you're a competent player, and therefore
your "i was able to!!" is going to get discounted. I don't think you
ever had to play against weenie POT decks packing Pulled Fangs and
burning every vamp they sent to torpor. I don't think you ever watched
POT/pro do almost the same thing. And I don't think you ever played
with big vamps against strong players who were out to WIN the game and
really knew how to do it.

When you do, you start to realize just how much of a liability big
vampires are, and how much of your deck has to be built around support
for them, and making up for the action disadvantage against weenies.
Making vampires easier to burn would just make it that much harder for
big vamps -- now you have to be SURE they don't hunt, or some weenie
with an Ivory Bow (or Claws) and a KRCG is going to toast you.

There. I insulted you again. Now what, Sam?

Google has significant problems with its usage. For instance, some
people use headers of the form:

From: <some...@trap.somewhere.invalid>
Reply-to: <a.r...@address.for.this.example>

Google won't obey those for replies, unless you go into the original
format etc., which isn't terribly useful.

Google is very slow. Posts made elsewhere can take hours to turn up.
This means that a thread that evolves in a matter of a few hours, with a
dozen people taking part, can be delayed hugely. You can't see the
responses to your article for another period of time.

Google requires you to be online. Downloading news to a local spool and
reading it there, offline, can be extremely useful. Since you can set
it up to download everything you want at the start, that can happen in a
minute or two (or more, depending on how many groups you read) and then
disconnect. With Google, you have to be online the whole time. This
isn't a cost issue (though that can have an effect) but, for people
using modems (as many people still do), this can be tying up their phone
line for a significant period of time.

Google - because of popular demand (it's notable that it was showing the
articles shortly after it bought the spools from Deja, it was showing
these posts) - has problems with anyone who uses X-No-Archive which is
perfectly valid for all sorts of reasons. Google also won't respect
Cancels, which are also valid for all sorts of reasons, but this is
becoming increasingly common on servers, due to cancel attacks and the
like.

You don't get to keep an archive of your own posts, for your own
purposes.

And so on.

Google is perfectly adequate for some usage patterns, but not for other
people. Working on a principle of "It works like this on Google" is
generally flawed. And even if you're using Google, you still have to
work out who's saying what if attributions aren't kept and threading is
randomly abused. That doesn't change. It's just the same as using a
local spool.

>> In this case, 5th Tradition compares quite favorably to hunting.

It depends.

There's less of a cost here with library inclusion and discard and time
in hand, of course, because it's a cardless action. By virtue of being
a cardless action, it's available to all vampires[0] so at any point you
can do it.

However, they do both compete for the resource of vampire actions.
(Primarily vampires, anyway.) Looking at an action from a point of view
of "This one is free and I can do it without it costing a library
resource" and "This one costs 1 blood, requires a Prince or Justicar and
gives me lots of blood" is a useful comparison for many players.

As with my thoughts on Delaying Tactics, which go "Am I better off
including this or including something else?", the thought of "Will I
better off *taking* this action, or using a default action and including
Blood Doll/Delaying Tactics/Direct Intervention/Sudden Reversal/Archon
Investigation?" isn't an altogether invalid one.

[0] Yes, there are restrictions on some vampires or the Blood Curse etc.
But talking in general.

another card) to bring into play, combat must occur, other cards must
be added
to it for it to burn a vampire.<<

These same restrictions apply to your vaunted Anathema, with the
additional issue of Anathama requiring a Prince/Justicar and then the
passing of a referendum.

>>Ivory Bow has all the same requirements and costs except for the
title and vote. It also has the 1 pool cost which Anathema does not.
It cannot burn vampires or gain pool.<<

You are trivializing the "except for the title and vote". The vampire
has to have a specific title, it has to take the political action
successfully and then make sure the referendum passes.

>>Majesty is a card that has been a staple card in the game since its
inception. Since it is one of the first cards - it defines what
balance is. It's cost and effect set the pace. It never was out of
balance.<<

The problem is, when Majesty was first designed there were fewer
vampires that could use it. Majesty was balanced in the beginning.
Now that so many (specifically so many small-capacity) vampires are
able to use it to effectively end combat at inferior has put Majesty
above the power curve.

Think of the card costs involved- beating the hell out of a vampire
most often requires several cards. Barring the few specific ways made
to combat Strike: Combat Ends (all of which besides Immortal Grapple
and Psyche! were from sets after Majesty's initial printing), Majesty
only requires one card to negate all that hard work a vampire put into
trying to beat the hell out of you. If a card is going to offer that
much card and time advantage, it would seem to require a non-renewable
cost of some kind.

For example, Skin of Steel (like Majesty) can negate several combat
cards by preventing all the damage from a strike. Deflection can
negate several bleed-related/action modifier cards. Both have a
non-renewable cost, to balance this fact so they cannot be as easily
cycled.

>>The basis for the rules change is that adding effect to cards that
use agg as an effect and adding cost to cards that use agg as a cost
would balance them better cost vs. effect when compared with other
cards.<<

Well, Daring the Dawn would instantly become wallpaper compared to Day
Operation, since Daring the Dawn would remove 1 blood at superior, and
can still be blocked by allies. How is that "balancing better"?
Except for a few cornercases where you're having fun with Masochism,
Day Operation would be better in every situation. With the current
rule, the cards have a comparable drawback- Daring doesn't remove
blood from the vamipre at superior, while Day Op always has a cost of
1 blood. Day Op is completely unblockable however. It's a balanced
situation.

So, I think you need to show that using agg as a cost needs to be
"balanced better cost vs. effect".

>>I have said that all deck archetypes were still viable when the
V:TES rule was
in effect.<<

Do you have any statistical information to support this claim?

>>I think it would be a change for the better. It would add more
exitement and drama to the game. And would not deter from the balance
of the game.<<

It would make combat more "dangerous", I will agree. However, making
it more "exciting and dramatic" is completely subjective. For me,
staying out of torpor is exciting enough, getting vampires burned
constantly would be frustrating and annoying.

>>The possibility that one's vamp might burn from playing Daring the
Dawn, does not take away from it's effect - it does not wallpaper the
card.<<

Actually it does, as shown above. Unless you're using Masochism, Day
Operation would be a better card in every way.

>>And while the rule would add to the effect of Ivory Bow without
increasing its cost - the card would still not be broken.<<

No, but it would likely hop up to the top of the power curve. While
you may feel that this change is more "exciting", it needs to be shown
why it is "necessary". Rules changes should not be made lightly and
certainly not because it would make one person's time in combat more
"exciting".

>>There are cards that can burn vamps (ie anathema, society of
leopold) that can burn vamps with little cost. Agg damage is never
free and cannot burn a vamp without being added to.<<

Agg damage most certainly can burn a vampire without being added to:
Burning Wrath, Walk of Flame, Breath of the Dragon, Flamethrower,
Improvised Flamethrower, Escaped Mental Patient, Dragon's Breath
Rounds, Body Flare, Mythic Form, Body of Sun, Taste of Death, Song in
the Dark, Blood Agony, Blood of Acid, Body Arsenal, Burst of Sunlight,
Compress, Conflaguration, Eruption of Vitae, and a whole mess of melee
weapons can burn a vampire without being added to. Several of these
cards (Dragon's Breath, Burst, Walk) have no blood or pool costs.
They may have opportunity costs, but so do Society and Anathema.

This might be your problem. Bear with me. This isn't an xCL rant.

Balanced, not balanced, fun, not fun, cheesy, not cheesy, Mr Suitcase or
Mr Handbag. There have been all sorts of arguments about xCL limited
environments over the years.

Bottom line: xCL creates environments which are quite different to NL
environments. People play them for whatever reasons they choose.

It may be useful to determine a better word than "balanced" to describe
the environment, however, due to its many multiple meanings in different
contexts already.

(If you want to have a discussion about the benefits and problems of
xCL, that's probably best off in a brand new thread.)

However, you have a house rule that, as one of its consequences, makes
it harder to access additional damage or large sources of aggravated
damage. This can be seen trivially: All 5CL decks and all 5CL
combinations of cards are accessible under NL. So even with the easiest
possible access (picking exactly the right vampires with exactly the
right disciplines), that access can be made easier under NL since there
are, currently, insufficient cards in the same discipline to make the
best possible NL distribution possible under xCL, where x is a low
number.

e.g. Under your deck, you can have 5 Ivory Bows (which is probably more
than enough). However, you can only have 5 Carrion Crows. So, you
might pick 2 Ivory Bows, 5 Carrion Crows, 3 Wolf Companions, maybe.

Under the official rules, I might pick 8 Carrion Crows, 2 Ivory Bows.
Or 10 Carrion Crows. For me, accessing a burn situation is now slightly
easier - I don't have to spend actions on Wolf Companions or Murder of
Crows (Murder might be better for ranged damage, here). Or I might pick
to play it exactly as you do. I have options, and some of those options
are going to make the situation easier, in any given situation.

So, under official rules, accessing the burn condition for an opposing
vampire in a given deck can be significantly easier.

Your House Rule, as one of its consequences, makes it harder to be
burned - accessing the cards is just that bit more difficult than it is
under NL.

Under your House Rule, changing the rules back to the V:TES rule might
not imbalance things.

However, rules changes are made for the official environment, both
rulebook and tournament in different situations (the two of which will
finally merge). In the official environment, burning vampires is
*already* easier than it is in your environment. Changing the rule back
to the V:TES print rule will make it easier *again*.

Your house rule pulls the power level of aggravated damage in general
down - due to the difficulty. You then add to it with another rules
change, which might put it back to balanced.

In the official environment, however, it is already seen as balanced.
Decks can and do use it, but decks don't need to use it. When the
option for it is there, it is rarely a no-brainer. Decks using it do
not win or lose disproportionately. And so on.

Changing the rules will then push the power level *up* from the current
de facto balance in the official situation. This pushes it towards
unbalanced.

Unfortunately, you are arguing for a change in the *official*
environment because your House Rule weakens something in a way you
didn't expect or foresee.

You may be better off adjusting your House Rule to a fashion you are
happy with. Those playing the official rules seem to be having no
problems with aggravated damage. You, playing your House Rule, are
having problems with it.

This leaves an obvious avenue for investigation - your house rule.

smoking, but continue to participate in the Marlboro Fan Club.

I've seen a few people about talking about an alternative league. I don't care
if I sound condescending, but I don't think any of them are capable of
organizing a sustainable opposition. The problem is that the game will move on
without them. When the MJL (later NJL) formed there hadn't been any new cards
in 2 years and 2 years later, shortly after new cards were released, we joined
back into the community at large because our core concern, errata being
released by new printed editions of cards rather than online only, had been
addressed. Realistically, we were going to be losing all of our leverage and
had to negotiate with LSJ while we arguably still had some.

None of the people complaining have provided _any_ logical proof that the set
grouping rule would unbalance the game or that the game would be balanced
without it. If I'm wrong, show me. I want to see numbers and graphs and I don't
want to see the ridiculous alternative of "don't print new vampires". The value
of your old cards in the secondary market isn't the responsibility of White
Wolf. If you bought V:TES cards because of their market value, rather than their
usefulness in a deck, then you are an idiot. V:TES cards aren't worth shit and
never have been.

For those of you still whining, let me quote Eric Cartman. Quit your bitching.
If you're not willing to back your complaints with action, there's no point in
pressing the buttons on your keyboard.
